lines: A screen copy of an Akai MIDIMix: every knob, fader and button on the controller gets a control here and an output jack, and the module drives the controller's button lamps back the other way
Follows one of the controller's 24 knobs and can be turned on screen as well; the hardware knob has no motor, so turning this one leaves the controller where it was until its next message arrives
That knob's position as 0-10V
Follows one of the controller's eight channel faders and can be moved on screen as well; the hardware fader has no motor, so moving this one leaves the controller where it was
That fader's position as 0-10V
Latches that strip's mute on and off; the matching lamp on the controller is driven to match, and pressing the controller's own button toggles it too
10V while that strip's mute is latched on, 0V while it is off
Latches that strip's record arm on and off; the matching lamp on the controller is driven to match, and pressing the controller's own button toggles it too
10V while that strip's record arm is latched on, 0V while it is off
Follows the controller's ninth fader and can be moved on screen as well
The ninth fader's position as 0-10V
Latches one of the controller's two bank buttons on and off, with the lamp under that button driven to match
Latches the controller's solo button on and off; that button has no lamp in the hardware, so only the screen shows its state
10V while that switch is latched on, 0V while it is off
Note — nothing arrives until a device is chosen: right-click and set both the MIDI input and the MIDI output to the MIDI Mix, because the output is what drives the lamps
Note — the controller never lights its own buttons, so this module holds the true button state and resends all eighteen lamps periodically; unplugging and replugging the controller resyncs on its own
Note — after loading a patch, press SEND ALL on the controller to push its knob and fader positions into the module, which cannot ask for them itself
Note — the red lamp at the top of the panel brightens whenever a MIDI message arrives and fades over about an eighth of a second, which is the quickest way to tell whether the device is talking
Menu — MIDI input (MIDIMix) — heads the chooser for the port the controller's knob, fader and button messages come in on
Menu — MIDI output (LEDs) — heads the chooser for the port the button lamp messages are sent out on; set it to the same device
Menu — Jitter filter (dead-band) — drops single-step changes from a noisy pot but accepts both extremes, so the full travel stays reachable

Powder.notes: Read at commit b3c1913, the only commit in the repository; its plugin.json is byte for byte the installed one, so the installed 2.0.0 is that commit. The README says 53 outputs; the module declares 52, which is also what its own list of controls adds up to, 24 knobs plus 9 faders plus 16 buttons plus 3 switches. Everything the module puts out comes from a parameter, so all 52 jacks work with no MIDI device attached at all and the controller only writes into those parameters. The screen-to-hardware direction covers lamps only: the two bank buttons and the sixteen mute and record-arm buttons are lit from here, while the knobs and faders cannot be moved from the screen because the hardware has no motors. The solo switch is deliberately not lit, which is what its tooltip, Switch 3 (no hardware LED), records. Nothing here is polyphonic. The panel prints no name on any control; the strip numbers 1 to 9 along the bottom are the only lettering.
